03 / EXPERIMENTS

Experimental Results

We evaluate our models across MCPMark, MCP-Atlas, and Toolathlon-Verified, and further use LOCA-bench at 8k–64k environment-state sizes. Each reported pass rate averages four independent runs.

ProgAgent uses PTC evaluation; the baselines in the main results table use DTC. MCPMark excludes the GitHub suite. Toolathlon scores marked † are from the original Toolathlon benchmark; all other scores in that column are from Toolathlon-Verified. “–” denotes an unreported score.

On MCPMark, ProgAgent achieves average pass rates of 18.3% at 8B and 29.7% at 14B, respectively. On Toolathlon-Verified, ProgAgent reaches 9.3% at 8B and 17.1% at 14B, compared with at most 2.8% and 1.9% among the 8B and 14B baselines.

Moreover, on MCP-Atlas, ProgAgent-14B achieves 45.6%, comparable to Claude Sonnet-4.5 (43.8%) under the DTC harness. The gap is most pronounced on LOCA-bench: the evaluated comparable-size baselines score zero at 32k and 64k, while ProgAgent mitigates context rot to maintain pass rates between 17.3% and 30.7% at 64k.

Training-data Scales

The resulting 215 tasks are each instantiated at 4 scales, yielding a shared training pool of 860 task instances.

Training Paradigms across Benchmarks

The table below compares each training recipe with its untrained backbone under the same harness. For untrained backbones, switching to PTC provides limited benefits across benchmarks and often yields the lowest scores among the three harnesses. Training reverses this pattern: after SFT and RL, the PTC recipe achieves the highest aggregate score on each benchmark at both model scales.

ProgAgent-14B reaches 29.7% on MCPMark and 45.6% on MCP-Atlas, compared with 8.0% and 29.7% for DTC, respectively. ProgAgent-8B also outperforms the 8B DTC model on all four benchmarks.

The chart above compares the three training paradigms on LOCA-bench, showing gains from both SFT and RL. As the environment state scales, DTC suffers from context rot. In contrast, PTC effectively mitigates this degradation and sustains robust performance, achieving average pass rates of 24.3% (8B) and 38.3% (14B). Furthermore, despite providing a more flexible action space during both training and evaluation, the Hybrid paradigm performs worse than PTC.

04 / ANALYSIS

Analysis

Training dynamicsEnvironment scalingTool orchestrationRemaining challenges
§5.1

What Does PTC Change During Training?

To understand how PTC changes agent behavior, we track the RL training dynamics of Qwen3-14B in the curves below. DTC achieves substantially lower rewards than PTC and Hybrid on our environments. Specifically, DTC’s reward increases only from 0.08 to 0.15, whereas the rewards of PTC and Hybrid start near 0.50 and reach 0.70 and 0.72, respectively.

For DTC, raw tool outputs account for around 30k context tokens per episode throughout training. Programmatic agents instead express orchestration as executable code, retain intermediate state in sandbox variables, and selectively print results. During RL training, the number of tool-output tokens under PTC decreases by roughly 20%, falling below 20k per episode; both programmatic paradigms also use roughly half as many tool calls as DTC.

PTC runtime errors per episode also decrease from 6.4 to 3.6 at 14B and from 7.5 to 5.0 at 8B. The 8B backbone reproduces the same trend (Appendix D.3).

§5.2

Does Environment State Scaling Help?

Environment state scaling provides a direct mechanism to control task difficulty for the DTC harness. As the environment state scales from v₀ to v₃, DeepSeek V4 Pro’s pass@8 under the DTC harness drops monotonically from 0.95 to 0.42 in the table below.

As shown in the full ablation results, restricting training from all four scales to the initial environments v₀ reduces average pass rates on LOCA-bench from 24.3% to 16.0% at 8B and from 38.3% to 23.7% at 14B. These results show that environment state scaling improves PTC performance on LOCA-bench across both backbones.

§5.3

How Does PTC Facilitate Tool Orchestration?

As shown in the table below, PTC models use a range of programming structures, including loops, conditional execution, and error handling, to orchestrate tools during RL.

To separate training effects from harness effects, we evaluate DTC- and PTC-trained models under both DTC and PTC harnesses on LOCA-bench and MCP-Atlas (see the cross-harness evaluation below). For DTC-trained models, switching from the DTC to the PTC harness improves performance on LOCA-bench but not on MCP-Atlas.

We also evaluate other baselines under the PTC harness. Their pass rates remain low (see the full ablation results), suggesting that access to the PTC interface alone is insufficient for effective orchestration.

Under the same PTC harness, PTC-trained models outperform DTC-trained models on both benchmarks. This advantage also holds under DTC evaluation: on MCP-Atlas, the 14B PTC-trained model outperforms its DTC-trained counterpart by 11.9 percentage points.

These results suggest that PTC training improves tool orchestration beyond the gains from the PTC harness alone, with benefits that extend to direct tool calling. This advantage persists under v₀-only training (see the full ablation results).

§5.4

What Challenges Remain for PTC Agents?

DTC-like behavior in complex environments: When environments return unpredictable or highly unstructured content, PTC agents may revert to DTC-like behavior. On Playwright, choosing the next tool call may require interpreting the current snapshot. For ProgAgent-14B, 40.7% of PTC calls contain a single tool invocation without control flow, error handling, or selective printing (see the interaction costs below). This behavior limits the benefits of programmatic orchestration and context management.

Silent server failures: The PTC harness of ProgAgent relies on MCP’s isError field to raise tool exceptions; however, non-compliant servers often omit this field, bypassing the agent’s exception-based recovery. Disabling this server-level error detection drops LOCA-bench pass rates from 24.3% to 19.3% at 8B and from 38.3% to 34.5% at 14B (see the full ablation results). Without explicit exceptions, the agent may process error messages as successful tool returns.

ABSTRACT

ProgAgent

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly expected to orchestrate diverse tools over long-horizon tasks. Existing agents typically use Direct Tool Calling (DTC), where the model invokes tools sequentially, and tool responses accumulate in the model context, which can lead to context rot and orchestration breakdown. In contrast, Programmatic Tool Calling (PTC) invokes tools through executable code and stores intermediate results in runtime variables rather than appending them to the context. Prior work has explored PTC mainly as an inference-time optimization, but its benefits for agentic training remain unclear, and suitable verifiable training tasks are scarce. In this work, we introduce ProgAgent, a full PTC training stack, comprising a pipeline for synthesizing verifiable long-horizon tasks, a lightweight PTC runtime, and a two-stage training recipe. Using only 215 tasks instantiated at four environment scales, ProgAgent yields higher pass rates than the evaluated baselines of comparable size across four benchmarks. On LOCA-bench, ProgAgent-14B achieves a 30.7% pass rate at a 64k-token environment state, where these baselines score zero. Cross-harness experiments show that PTC-trained models outperform DTC-trained models under both evaluation interfaces, suggesting that the benefits of PTC training extend beyond the interface. We will release the model checkpoints and task synthesis pipeline.
